lines.text: Freedom of education.
In the Netherlands you may choose the school for your child yourself, if there is a place there.

There are Christian and Islamic schools, public schools [openbare] ('openbaar' means public, for everyone; your religion is not important), and schools with a different system, for example a jenaplanschool.
Compulsory education from five to sixteen.
Compulsory education [Leerplicht] means that children must go to school.
From the age of four almost all children go to primary school, but from five years old it is mandatory [verplicht].
The leerplicht lasts until a child is sixteen; whoever turns sixteen must still finish the school year.
Children of sixteen and seventeen without a diploma must also go to school; that is called being obliged to obtain a qualification [kwalificatieplichtig] — the vmbo diploma is not enough.
Free only during holidays.
A child only has time off during a school holiday.
For an extra holiday or a celebration a child does not get time off; if you stay home anyway, you can get a fine [boete].
If your child is sick, you must call the school yourself in the morning.
Obligations for the school.
Every school gets regular inspections, for example on the quality [kwaliteit] of the education and the number of lesson hours.
Schools are required to teach about Dutch society [samenleving] and about sexual development [seksuele ontwikkeling] — for example about puberty.
Children also learn that homoseksualiteit is accepted in the Netherlands.
What does the school expect from parents?
Contact between parents and school is important.

It can happen like this: dropping in to the classroom; parents' evenings [ouderavonden] — information for parents; a few times a year a 10-minute talk [10-minutengesprek] with the teacher, often with test results and a school report [rapport].
Schools sometimes ask parents to help, for example with a school trip [schoolreisje] — that is voluntary [vrijwillig].
